Welcome to the Reverse Engineering module! In this lesson, you will learn how to extract hidden information from Android applications.

• APKTool - Decompiles APK files
• Jadx - Java decompiler
• dex2jar - Converts DEX to JAR
• JD-GUI - Java class viewer
• Android Studio - APK Analyzer

1. Static Analysis - Examine code without running
2. String Search - Look for hardcoded values
3. Network Analysis - Monitor API calls
4. Decompilation - Convert bytecode to source

• Check strings.xml for hardcoded text
• Look in BuildConfig and resource files
• Examine obfuscated code carefully
• Use grep to search decompiled code
• Check native libraries (.so files)
Find the flag hidden in plain sight within this application. Use static analysis tools to decompile the APK and search through the code.
Hint: The flag is stored as a simple string constant in one of the Java classes. Try searching for "flag" or "key" in the decompiled code.
This flag has been encoded to make it slightly harder to find. You\'ll need to decode it after finding it in the source code.
Hint: Look for Base64 encoded strings or other common encoding schemes. The flag might be split across multiple variables or methods.
That\'s not right. Check your decoding.
The hardest challenge yet! The flag is obfuscated and split across multiple locations. You\'ll need advanced reverse engineering skills.
Hint: The flag is constructed at runtime using multiple obfuscated methods. Look for string concatenation, XOR operations, or reflection. Try debugging or analyzing the bytecode.
Incorrect. This one requires deep analysis.

Learn about insecure data storage vulnerabilities in mobile applications. This is one of the most common security issues in mobile apps where sensitive information is stored without proper protection.

Insecure data storage occurs when sensitive information like passwords, tokens, personal data, or cryptographic keys are stored on the device without adequate protection. Attackers with physical access to the device or malware can extract this data.

• SQLite Databases (unencrypted)
• SharedPreferences (plain text)
• Internal Storage files
• External Storage (SD card)
• Application logs
• Temporary files
• Cloud storage backups

1. Physical Access - Anyone with the device can extract data
2. Backup Exposure - Data in cloud backups
3. Malware - Other apps can access unprotected data
4. Forensics - Data persists even after app deletion
5. Rooted Devices - Full filesystem access

• Use ADB to pull app data directory
• Examine SQLite databases with sqlite3
• Check SharedPreferences XML files
• Review app logs with logcat
• Use tools like Objection or Frida
• Inspect backup files
⚠️ WARNING: This is an intentionally vulnerable mobile application!

This app is part of the OWASP Security Shepherd Project - a web and mobile application security training platform.

Security Shepherd is designed to foster and improve security awareness among a varied skill-set demographic. The aim is to educate users about application security through hands-on challenges.

This mobile app contains intentional security vulnerabilities for educational purposes. Do NOT install this on a device with sensitive data.

This challenge contains a SQLite database with multiple user accounts. The passwords are stored in an encoded format. Your mission is to extract the database, decode the passwords, and find the flag.\n\nThe key is not in the UI - it\'s hidden in the database!

1. Use ADB to pull the app's database files
2. The database is named "Users.db"
3. Passwords appear to be encoded
4. Look for Base64 encoding
5. One of the decoded passwords is the flag

This challenge stores a password hash in a SQLite database. Unlike simple encoding, this password has been hashed using MD5. Your task is to crack the hash and recover the original password.\n\nThe key is not in the UI - crack the hash!

1. Extract the passwordDB.db database using ADB
2. The password is stored as an MD5 hash
3. MD5 is a weak hashing algorithm
4. Use online rainbow tables or tools like hashcat
5. Hash: 0e3a0c8c3a571a855c958813d9b851a1

This challenge stores sensitive credentials in Android SharedPreferences. Many developers think this is secure, but SharedPreferences files are stored as plain XML and can be easily extracted.\n\nYour mission: Extract the SharedPreferences XML file and find the secret flag among the stored credentials.

1. Use ADB to pull SharedPreferences files
2. Location: /data/data/com.owasp.reverser/shared_prefs/
3. File name: UserCredentials.xml
4. SharedPreferences stores everything in plain text XML
5. Look for a key named "secret_flag"
6. Command: adb pull /data/data/com.owasp.reverser/shared_prefs/UserCredentials.xml

This challenge implements custom encryption using a XOR cipher. While the data appears encrypted, the encryption scheme is weak and can be reverse engineered.\n\nYour mission: Decompile the APK, analyze the encryption algorithm, and decrypt the flag. This challenge requires understanding of cryptographic weaknesses.

1. Decompile the APK using jadx or apktool
2. Find the InsecureData4Fragment class
3. Analyze the xorEncrypt() method
4. The XOR key is hardcoded as "SHEPHERD"
5. XOR is symmetric - encryption and decryption are identical
6. Use the encrypted hex data shown in the app
7. Decrypt: ciphertext XOR key = plaintext
Poor authentication is one of the most critical mobile vulnerabilities. Authentication is the cornerstone of app security - if attackers bypass it, all other security measures become irrelevant.

• Weak security questions (easily guessable)
• Passwords logged in plaintext
• Credentials in world-readable files
• Weak temporary passwords
• Verbose error messages
• Debug logs in production

Why Security Questions Fail:

• Answers often public (social media)
• Easy to guess or research
• Predictable common answers
• Never change over time

Better Alternatives:
• Email-based password reset
• SMS one-time codes
• Biometric authentication

Logging Dangers:

• Logcat accessible via ADB
• World-readable files
• Logs persist after deletion
• Cloud backups expose data

Never Log:
• Passwords, PINs, tokens
• API keys
• Personal information
• Security answers

Secure Practices:

• Strong password policies
• Multi-factor authentication
• Email verification for resets
• Account lockout after failures
• Never log credentials
• Disable debug logs in production

This challenge demonstrates multiple poor authentication vulnerabilities:

• Weak security questions with easily discoverable answers
• Sensitive information logged to logcat
• Personal details written to files
• Weak temporary password generation

Your mission: The account is locked, but you can use the password reset feature. Find the security question answers by examining logs and files, reset the password, login, and capture the flag!

Hint: Start by checking logcat for interesting information...

Inadequate supply chain security occurs when mobile apps use vulnerable third-party libraries, SDKs, or dependencies. Attackers exploit these weak links to compromise entire applications, affecting millions of users.

Third-Party Risks:

• Outdated libraries with known CVEs
• Malicious code in dependencies
• Hardcoded credentials in SDKs
• Unvetted third-party components
• Supply chain attacks (compromised updates)
• Backdoors in vendor libraries

Common Issues:

• Using dependencies with known vulnerabilities
• Not verifying SDK authenticity
• Hardcoded API keys in libraries
• Insecure data collection by third parties
• Excessive permissions requested by SDKs
• Outdated dependencies not updated for years

Secure Practices:

• Regularly audit and update dependencies
• Use dependency scanning tools (OWASP Dependency-Check)
• Verify checksums and signatures
• Monitor CVE databases
• Remove unused dependencies
• Review third-party SDK permissions
• Implement secure update mechanisms
• Use Software Bill of Materials (SBOM)

This app uses a vulnerable third-party analytics SDK from "ThirdPartyAnalytics Inc." The SDK is severely outdated (16 months old) and contains multiple security issues:

• Known CVEs (CVE-2023-45678, CVE-2024-12345)
• Hardcoded backdoor authentication token
• Insecure telemetry data storage
• Base64-encoded credentials in logs

Your mission: Analyze the SDK initialization process, examine logcat logs, inspect the app's files directory, and find the hidden flag that proves you've successfully exploited the supply chain vulnerability!

Hint: Use logcat filtering and explore the app's data directory using Device File Explorer or ADB.

Insecure communication occurs when mobile apps transmit sensitive data without proper encryption. Any attacker on the same network can intercept, read, and modify unencrypted traffic, leading to credential theft, session hijacking, and data breaches.

HTTP vs HTTPS:

• HTTP: Plaintext protocol - all data visible to anyone monitoring the network
• HTTPS: Encrypted with TLS/SSL - protects data confidentiality and integrity
• Mixed content: Using both HTTP and HTTPS exposes users to attacks
• Certificate validation: Must verify server identity to prevent MITM attacks

Common Issues:

• Sending credentials over HTTP
• Accepting invalid/self-signed certificates
• Using weak cipher suites or deprecated TLS versions
• Disabling certificate pinning for convenience
• Sensitive data in URLs (visible in logs/history)
• Mixed HTTP/HTTPS sessions exposing session tokens

Secure Practices:

• Always use HTTPS for all network communications
• Validate SSL/TLS certificates properly
• Implement certificate pinning for critical APIs
• Use strong cipher suites (TLS 1.2+)
• Never disable certificate validation in production
• Keep sensitive data out of URLs
• Use secure WebSocket (WSS) for real-time communication

This app makes multiple network requests to different endpoints. Some use HTTPS (secure), while others use HTTP (insecure).

Your mission: Monitor the app's network traffic using logcat, identify which requests are sent over HTTP, and extract the session token that was transmitted in plaintext.

Hints:
• Use logcat filter tag: AppNetworkMonitor
• Look for HTTP (not HTTPS) requests
• The flag is in the X-Session-Token header
• Pay attention to protocol warnings

Insufficient cryptography occurs when mobile apps use weak encryption algorithms, inadequate key lengths, poor key management, or flawed cryptographic implementations. These weaknesses allow attackers to decrypt sensitive data, bypass encryption, or manipulate cryptographic processes.

Common Crypto Vulnerabilities:

• Weak algorithms: DES, RC4, MD5, SHA-1
• Insufficient key length: Keys < 128 bits
• ECB mode: Pattern analysis attacks
• Hardcoded keys: Keys in source code
• Static IVs: Initialization vector reuse
• Weak key derivation: Simple hashing for keys
• Insecure random: Predictable Random() instead of SecureRandom
• No salt: Password hashing without random salt

Secure Cryptography Practices:

• Use AES-256 for symmetric encryption
• Use RSA-2048+ or ECC for asymmetric crypto
• Always use CBC, CTR, or GCM mode (never ECB)
• Generate random IVs for each encryption
• Use SecureRandom for all cryptographic values
• Store keys in Android Keystore
• Use PBKDF2, bcrypt, or scrypt for key derivation
• Always salt password hashes
• Use SHA-256 or SHA-3 for hashing
• Implement proper key rotation
• Never hardcode cryptographic keys

Real-World Consequences:

• Data Breaches: Encrypted data exposed when weak crypto is cracked
• Compliance Violations: GDPR, PCI-DSS require strong encryption
• Financial Loss: Credit card theft, fraud from decrypted data
• Reputation Damage: Loss of customer trust
• Intellectual Property Theft: Competitors access proprietary algorithms

Example: In 2019, a banking app used DES encryption. Researchers cracked it in 6 hours, exposing millions of customer accounts.

This app implements cryptographic operations with multiple severe vulnerabilities:

• ECB Mode: Electronic Codebook mode reveals patterns in encrypted data
• MD5 Key Derivation: Using broken MD5 hash to generate encryption keys
• Insecure Random: Predictable Random() with fixed seed instead of SecureRandom
• Static IV: Reusing the same Initialization Vector for all encryptions

Your mission: Analyze the cryptographic implementation by monitoring logcat logs, decompile the APK to examine the crypto code, identify all vulnerabilities, and extract the hidden flag!

Hints:
• Filter logcat with tag: InsufficientCryptoChallenge
• Look for cipher suite, key derivation method, IV usage
• Use jadx to decompile and search for crypto-related classes
• The flag is obfuscated in byte arrays in the source code
